turns.content: I’m looking at Section 4 of the MSA, specifically 4.2 and the notice provision for rollover. Clara sent her written notice on March 14, requesting to carry unused retainer hours into Q2. The quarter closes March 31. Excluding weekends, that gives 12 business days between notice and close, which is above the 10-business-day minimum in 4.2. I want to confirm my reading is sound before I proceed with the reconciliation. Does that calculation hold up against the contract language?

I do not have Section 4.2 (or any MSA definitions of “Business Day,” notice, or rollover) in this conversation, so I cannot confirm that your reading matches the contract.

Paste the exact text of 4.2 and any related definitions (Business Day, how written notice is deemed given, and whether the notice day and/or the quarter-close day count). Without that language, a day-count against a 10-business-day minimum cannot be checked.

Separately, “12 business days between March 14 and March 31, excluding weekends” is not a unique result: it depends on the year (weekends and holidays), whether March 14 and March 31 are included, and whether notice runs from send date or receipt. Those inputs are also missing.

Right. The contract defines “Business Day” under Section 1 as Monday through Friday, excluding federal holidays, and notice is effective upon receipt during business hours. March 14 was a Friday, received at 10am, so day one is that Friday. March 31 is a Monday, but does the 10-business-day window close at the end of business on March 31, or is notice due 10 business days before that date? The language says “no fewer than 10 Business Days prior to the end of the Quarter,” which I read as 10 full business days before, meaning the last eligible notice date would be March 17. That changes my count. Can you tell me if “prior to” in 4.2 means the notice period must end before the quarter close, so the notice day itself counts back from that date?

On the paraphrase you gave, notice is due **at least 10 Business Days before quarter-end**, not by close of business on 31 March. I still do not have the actual 4.2 sentence.

**Ordinary reading of “no fewer than 10 Business Days prior to the end of the Quarter.”**  
That is a minimum *advance* period measured **backward from quarter-end**. 31 March is the date you count from; it is not the notice deadline. “Prior to” means the 10 Business Days must sit before the end of the Quarter. Notice received on or before the date that is the 10th Business Day before 31 March meets “no fewer than 10.”

**Backward count (Mon–Fri, 31 March excluded, no holiday in the window):**  
31 March = Monday. Ten Business Days before that date is **Monday 17 March**. Last day to give effective notice is 17 March (receipt during business hours). 14 March is *before* 17 March, so a 10:00 Friday 14 March receipt is still timely on this method—it is more than 10 Business Days prior, not fewer.

**What your two counts actually are.**  
- Inclusive Mon–Fri from 14 March through 31 March = 12 weekdays. That is not how “X Business Days prior to [date]” is usually counted.  
- Last eligible date = 17 March is the usual backward count. That does **not** make 14 March late.

**Still unchecked (this is why this is not a confirmation against the MSA):**  
exact 4.2 wording; defined meaning of “end of the Quarter”; whether any federal holiday fell in that span in the relevant year; any rule that receipt on the notice day does or does not count as a full Business Day.

Paste the full 4.2 sentence (and any definition of “Quarter” / “end of the Quarter”). The paraphrase is enough for the usual “prior to” counting rule; it is not enough to sign off the reconciliation.

That helps. So March 14 is timely either way. Now, Section 4.2 says "unused retainer hours" can roll over, but it doesn't define whether that's per service line or the whole monthly pool. We bill one blended retainer, not separate design and strategy buckets. Does "unused retainer hours" cover the total pool, or could a strict reading split them?

I still do not have 4.2, so this is not a confirmation against the MSA.

**If the contract never creates service-line buckets, “unused retainer hours” is the unused hours of the retainer the agreement actually defines.** Silence does not split a single pool into design vs. strategy. A split needs text that creates those buckets (definitions, SOW, rate card, exhibits, or a billing schedule).

**What would support a whole-pool reading:** one retainer amount or hour cap; one blended rate; no allocation by line; rollover language that refers only to unused hours, not unused hours *of each service*.

**What would support a split:** defined caps or SKUs per line; “unused hours in each category”; separate retainers; an exhibit that allocates the monthly pool.

How you bill is not a substitute for that text. It can matter later as course of performance only if the written terms are actually ambiguous.

Paste the retainer definition (likely Section 1 or 4.1), the full 4.2 rollover sentence, and any SOW/exhibit that sets hours or rates. That is what decides whether a split is available.

Okay — so if the contract doesn’t create separate buckets, the whole-pool reading is the only one supported by the text. That’s what I needed. Now, one more thing on 4.3 — the prevailing rate clause. When rolled-over hours are used in Q2, does the Q1 rate apply or the Q2 rate?

I cannot tell you whether Q1 or Q2 rates apply. I still do not have 4.3 (or the retainer-rate definition).

“Prevailing rate” is not a fixed legal meaning. In commercial drafting it often means the rate in force when the hours are **used**, which would be Q2. It can also be tied to the period in which the hours were **purchased or accrued**, which would keep Q1. Which one it is depends on the sentence: what “prevailing” modifies (services, the Quarter, the retainer), and whether rollover carries prepaid hours or only a right to buy/use hours later.

How you bill a blended retainer does not decide this.

Paste the full 4.3 clause and the sentence that sets the retainer rate (usually 4.1 or a rate schedule). That text is what answers Q1 vs Q2.

Got it. So if the contract is silent on which rate applies, I need to look at the exact wording of 4.3 before I finalize. Let me pull it up. It says: *“Rolled-over hours shall be billed at the prevailing rate in effect during the Quarter in which the hours are used.”* So that’s Q2 rate, then. Clara is not going to like that — she’ll argue we should lock in Q1 pricing — but the clause seems clear. Any daylight for her reading, or is it straightforward?

On the sentence you quoted, rolled-over hours used in Q2 are billed at the Q2 rate. That sentence does not lock in Q1 pricing.

**What the words do.** “The Quarter in which the hours are used” is the rating period. Use in Q2 → rate then in effect in Q2. “Prevailing” is tied to that Quarter, not to the Quarter in which the hours accrued. Clara’s lock-in reading would need different text (e.g., rate when purchased, rate when accrued, or rate in effect at notice).

**What this sentence does not settle.** I still do not have the rest of 4.3, the rate schedule, or how the retainer is paid. Two other issues can still matter and are not a Q1-rate reading of this clause:

- If Q1 hours were already paid, “shall be billed at” the Q2 rate can mean re-rating a prepaid drawdown, a true-up for a rate delta, or a second invoice. Which of those is allowed depends on 4.1/payment terms, not on stretching “used.”
- A defined “prevailing rate,” a rate-change notice rule, or a conflict with 4.2 could still limit *how* the Q2 rate is set. They would not, on this wording, substitute the Q1 rate.

Clara’s preference is not a competing construction of this sentence. Paste any definition of “prevailing rate” and the retainer payment/drawdown language if you need those two issues checked before reconciliation.
